title: Chinese philosophy exposes the limits of AI creativity
subtitle: Real creativity requires a living, perceiving body
author: Davide Andrea Zappulli
introduction: Investors are betting that AI can replace human creators. China’s AI movie industry is already valued at $3bn, and the American AI music-generation company Suno reached a $5.4bn valuation this year. This raises the question of whether there is anything unique about human creativity. Philosopher Davide Andrea Zappulli draws on Chinese philosophy to argue that human creativity isn’t just the recombining of old ideas, as machines do. It’s seeing reality in new ways, which requires a living body that interacts with the world and experiments with different ways of grasping it. Consequently, genuine creativity is beyond AI.
body:
Creativity plays a central role in contemporary culture. As the philosopher Berys Gaut puts it, “our culture is obsessed with creativity.” And no wonder! Creativity is a driving force behind development in science, technology, and the arts. We also value creativity in our personal lives, read books about how to unlock our creative potential, and desire an education system capable of fostering it. At the same time, recent developments in artificial intelligence have started to threaten our confidence in the importance of human creative capacities. Is human creativity distinct or unique in some way? If not, what is its future in the age of AI?

To address these and other issues, we need to understand what creativity is and how it arises. Yet, doing this has proven to be remarkably difficult. While, at a general level, there is wide agreement that creativity is the capacity to generate ideas that are new and valuable, philosophers and psychologists have struggled to figure out how we generate such ideas and what kind of mental processes realize our creative capacities. In fact, some have gone as far as proposing the extreme view that creativity lies beyond explanation. For example, Immanuel Kant argued that since any explanation is given by reference to rules, and creativity is precisely what cannot be captured by rules, it is in the nature of creativity that it cannot be explained.

Some say that it is in the hardest battles that uniting forces is most needed. If so, explaining creativity might be the kind of enterprise in which integrating resources from different philosophical traditions could play a vital role. In particular, some help might come from one of the most influential texts in the Chinese philosophical tradition: the Zhuangzi.

The Zhuangzi took shape in ancient China during the second half of the Warring States period (475–221 BCE). This is the foundational period of Chinese philosophy, which witnessed the start of the schools of Confucianism, Daoism, Mohism, and Legalism. (This taxonomy is anachronistic, but we don’t need to get into that here.) The Zhuangzi is classified, albeit anachronistically, as a Daoist text. It is also a work of a singular kind, departing from other texts of the time in its peculiarly imaginative style—full of evocative stories, jokes, talking animals, and descriptions of wondrous metamorphoses. It is precisely where we might expect to find insights about creativity.

One such story occurs in the first chapter. There, Huizi (Zhuangzi’s friend) tells the character Zhuangzi that he has received a gourd as a present from the king of the state of Wei. Yet, the gourd was a very special one—so huge that it weighed more than 100 pounds! Asked by Zhuangzi what he did with it, Huizi replies:

I tried to make it into a water container, but it was so heavy that I could not lift it anymore. I then split it to make a ladle, but it was too big to scoop into anything. […] It’s not that it wasn’t spacious and so big, but there was nothing I could use it for and so I destroyed it.

Upon hearing this, Zhuangzi replies:

The master here is set in his ways when it comes to using big things. […] How could you not think of making it into a big vessel to float in the rivers and lakes instead of getting concerned about its size? The master’s mind seems to be all tangled up! (My translations.)

In this story, Huizi is clearly depicted as failing to act well. But why? Well, his failure is precisely a failure of creativity. In ancient China, gourds were typically used to make utensils like containers and ladles. Accordingly, what Huizi does is nothing but run through the ways of conceiving of gourds that he had learned from his society and culture. When none of those works for the unusually large specimen, he is stuck, incapable of coming up with a new and effective use for the gourd. Conversely, Zhuangzi’s proposal shows what an ideal agent would have done: adapt to the unusual circumstance by coming up with a new use for the gourd that is effective in that situation.

In the Zhuangzi, creativity is important because it is the capacity allowing us to adapt to changing circumstances. The question is then what the Zhuangzi takes creativity to be. Most accounts of creativity in contemporary philosophy and psychology locate the creative process in high-level cognition. For example, in her influential book The Creative Mind, Margaret Boden proposes that creativity takes place at the level of conceptual schemas, understanding the creative process as consisting of operations by which one combines ideas one already possesses to generate new ones.

Interestingly, that is exactly what AI systems like large language models do: they compose tokens that they already possess in order to produce new instances of text. In fact, in providing her theory of creativity, Boden takes the standpoint of what is known as the “computational theory of the mind,” understanding mental processes—at least many of them—as the kind of processes that occur in computers. Once one takes this approach, the step towards attributing creativity to AI systems and seeing our creativity as substitutable is quite short. On the contrary, as I have argued, the Zhuangzi contains a different account that envisions creativity as a more fundamental capacity that is rooted in perception, and particularly as a capacity that is a prerogative of living beings.

This account is based on a central idea of the text: that the way we see reality involves a constructive role on our part. One of the terms that the Zhuangzi uses to describe reality is “tianli” (天理). The first character (“tian 天”) can be translated as “heavenly” or “natural,” while the second (“li 理”) can be rendered as “pattern” or “structure.” As the philosopher Franklin Perkins has argued, the first of these two characters should be understood in opposition to the concept of human—by saying that reality has a heavenly structure, the Zhuangzi implies that there is a way the world is independently of our purposes, interests, and practices. At the same time, the Zhuangzi also describes reality as a “big clump” (dakuai 大塊), which implies that the world can be, so to speak, carved up in different ways. Taken together, these ideas lead to the following claim: there is a way the world is, but that way is such that it underdetermines how we are to represent it.

An analogy will help make the view clearer. If you are into thriller movies, you have probably encountered the Rorschach test, also known as the inkblot test. Initially developed to assess personality, the test consists of presenting participants with inkblots and asking them what they see in them. What matters for our purposes is that the same inkblot can be seen—and in fact will typically be seen—in different ways by different participants. A single subject can also switch between ways of seeing it over time. We can thus say that the inkblot underdetermines how we are to represent it. At the same time, it is not the case that anything goes. Clearly, there is a way the inkblot is—it is composed of certain colors and shapes, for instance—and that way puts constraints on the available ways of representing it. In sum, there is a way the inkblot is, but that way allows for many ways of representing it.

At least in the case at hand, this shows that representation comes with a constructive component. For the inkblot to underdetermine how we are to represent it is for there to be a gap between the way in which what is represented is and the way in which we represent it. By representing it one way as opposed to another, we close this gap, constructing what we represent in a certain way.

The idea of the Zhuangzi is that this kind of representational underdetermination does not happen only in paradigmatic cases like that of the inkblot. Rather, it is a ubiquitous feature of our engagement with the world. An example of this comes up in the dialogue between Zhuangzi and Huizi above, for seeing the gourd as a material for making a water container and seeing it as a vessel to float in the rivers and lakes are different ways of representing the same object. Another passage in the second chapter of the Zhuangzi goes as follows:

As paths form as they are walked, things are so by being called in a certain way. […] Things have certainly a place from which they are so. Things have certainly a place from which they are allowable. There is no thing that is not so. There is no thing that is not allowable. (My translation.)

As I read this passage, by saying that “things are so by being called in a certain way,” the Zhuangzi is recognizing the constructive element in representation. While this view might strike one as abstruse at first sight, it actually finds an ally in contemporary research in embodied cognition, and particularly in the view known as “enactivism.” As argued by Francisco Varela, Evan Thompson, and Eleanor Rosch in The Embodied Mind—arguably the foundational text of the enactive approach—perception does not consist of passively *re-*presenting subject-independent properties of the world. Rather, in perceiving we are actively constructing our experience, and we do so in an action-based way. In other words, the ways in which we construct the world around us in perception stem from the available ways of acting in the world, which are in turn determined by our natural and acquired capacities together with the subject-independent features of the world in which we live. Such an action-based theory of perception is also sympathetic to the Zhuangzi, as various passages in the text link different ways of representationally constructing the world to different functions or uses (yong 用) of the things around us that we can access.

The crucial idea is then this: the fact that reality underdetermines how we are to represent it leaves space for us to switch between different ways of constructing it. Moreover, in switching between different ways of constructing reality, we can access ways of doing so that are new and effective, as when Zhuangzi comes up with the idea of using the gourd as a vessel to float in the rivers and lakes. On this account, then, creativity ultimately consists of our capacity to construct the world in our perception. This capacity has the freedom to execute an incredible multitude of constructions, and to do so in a way that allows us to adapt to the reality around us. For the Zhuangzi, creativity is a perpetual dance between us and the world on the stage of perception.

An example of the exercise of this creativity comes in the third chapter. Surprisingly, the model of creativity we find there is a butcher, known as Ding. Ding is described as carving oxen with movements so fluid that a lord asks him how it is possible for skill to reach such perfection. Ding replies:

I encounter the ox with my spirit instead of examining it with the eyes […], relying on the heavenly structure, striking into the big gaps, guided by the big openings, and adapting to what is firmly so. (My translation.)

Butcher Ding is, indeed, an example of creativity. The reason his skill is so advanced is that he does not slice oxen by simply following some pre-determined set of rules. Rather, he is perfectly adaptable to the particular ox he encounters. Instead of merely applying concepts that he already possesses, Ding representationally constructs each ox on the go. By doing so, he can slice each ox perfectly because in each case he can generate new ways of conceiving it that are effective in the particular situation. As such, Ding’s practice is a creative one.

The passage gives us an even more specific idea of the mental process Ding executes. We said that creativity consists of the capacity to navigate between different ways of constructing the world. But how is it achieved? The answer lies in Ding’s claim that he relies on the heavenly structure, namely the subject-independent features of reality. Given that creativity is based in our capacity to representationally construct the world around us and that this construction takes as a basis the world’s subject-independent features, a process allowing us to navigate between different constructions has to be constituted of two phases. First, a phase that allows us to loosen our pre-existing construction of the situation, thereby accessing (or getting closer to accessing) subject-independent properties of the world as such. Second, a phase in which, so to speak, we move up again to the level of representational construction, potentially getting at novel ways of carving up the situation we are in.

In conclusion, the bottom line need not be that high-level thought cannot be creative. Arguably, there are many instances in which it is. Rather, the point is that there is a more fundamental kind of creativity which operates already in the way the world manifests itself to us. This fundamental kind of creativity is the capacity to navigate different ways of constructing the reality around us. It is the capacity to access different and novel ways of seeing the world.
